summary: Summation No. 16 covers non-military activities in Japan for January 1947 (with many statistics for December and November 1946). Politically it records Prime Minister Yoshida's failed coalition talks with the Social Democrats, the 31 January cabinet reshuffle, the extension of the purge to local government and key economic posts, the dissolution of neighborhood associations, and the Supreme Commander's 31 January ban on the planned 1 February general strike of about 2,000,000 government workers. War crimes sections report Yokohama and Philippine trials and the close of the prosecution case before the International Military Tribunal on 24 January, with extensive POW testimony. Economic sections document acute coal and electric power shortages, textile recovery with imported American cotton, trade with Korea, China and the United States, rationing, rice collection, finance and property control. Social sections cover earthquake relief, repatriation, disease rates, nutrition surveys, vital statistics and education reform. Useful for labor history, the purge, and the 1946 food and fuel crisis.
highlights: Yoshida's coalition talks with the Social Democrats failed (15-17 January and again later); on 31 January four ministers left and four were transferred, Etsujiro Uyehara became Home Minister and Yoshida temporarily took Agriculture and Forestry.

Imperial Ordinances Nos. 1-3 of 4 January extended the purge to local government and specified economic and media posts, with penalties up to 15,000 yen or three years; about 80,700 persons were scheduled for screening February-April.

On the night of 31 January the Supreme Commander prohibited the 1 February general strike planned by the All-Japan Joint Struggle Committee (about 30 organizations, some 4,000,000 workers), citing the risk of starvation to the Japanese people.

On 22 January the Government announced a Wage Investigation Commission, a cash wage limit raised from 500 to 700 yen, and temporary government worker raises of 150 yen plus 25 percent of base pay, which the unions rejected.

The prosecution closed its case before the International Military Tribunal for the Far East on 24 January after nine months, with extensive POW testimony; the defense opened 27 January, and Admiral Nagano had died on 5 January.

December coal output was 2,172,900 metric tons, yet coal and electric power shortages kept throttling industry; Bank of Japan notes reached 100,040,145,000 yen on 31 January and the national debt stood at 255,307,000,000 yen.

The 21 December earthquake killed 1,321, left 227 missing and destroyed 19,418 buildings in 25 prefectures; 62,784 Japanese were repatriated from 1 to 26 January, with 1,254,432 still awaiting return from Soviet-controlled areas.

First exports made from postwar American cotton (yarn to Hongkong and Burma) and first postwar fish oil to the United States shipped, while Antarctic whaling fleets caught 422 whales from 1 to 27 January.
keywords: International Military Tribunal for the Far East

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover for Summation No. 16 (January 1947), the contents of the four parts, and the list of 108 charts, maps and graphs.

sections.title: Part I: General
sections.summary: Digest of the month: no change in SCAP's non-military organization, Yoshida's failed coalition talks, the 31 January cabinet reshuffle, economic shortages, the 1 February strike crisis, earthquake relief and repatriation.

sections.title: Section 1. Organization under SCAP
sections.summary: Reports that the non-military organization of GHQ SCAP did not change during January 1947.

sections.title: Section 2. Political Activities
sections.summary: Yoshida's coalition talks collapsed and the cabinet was reshuffled on 31 January; the Diet session was delayed, the Constitution publicized, neighborhood associations dissolved, and police, prison and war crimes matters noted.

sections.title: Section 3. Economic Activities
sections.summary: Digest of resources, industry, textiles, labor, trade, rationing, finance and property control, including 1,100 tons of crude rubber arriving 20 January and the 15 January formation of the Joint Struggle Committee.

sections.title: Section 4. Social Activities
sections.summary: Digest of welfare, Red Cross earthquake relief, 62,784 repatriates, disease and vital statistics, education measures, religion, and information programs on the new Constitution.

sections.title: Part II: Political
sections.summary: Politics, public safety and war crimes: Yoshida's coalition efforts and 31 January reshuffle, the purge extended by 4 January ordinances, demonstrations and black-market raids, and the Tokyo war crimes trial.

sections.title: Section 1. Government and Politics
sections.summary: MacArthur's New Year statement, failed coalition negotiations, Diet Law features, the 91st Diet session summary, the extended purge ordinances and the abolition of tonari-gumi.

sections.title: Supreme Commander's New Year Statement
sections.summary: Full text of MacArthur's New Year message, praising 1946 reforms and warning that the new Constitution and land reform depend on the Japanese people's own use of their rights.

sections.title: Tenets of Occupation Policy
sections.summary: Japanese reaction to MacArthur's letters saying Christian ideals guide occupation policy, including a Nippon Times editorial of 6 January on Japan's spiritual vacuum.

sections.title: Political Developments
sections.summary: Yoshida's New Year speech attacking malcontents, two failed coalition attempts (17 January and later), and the 31 January cabinet reshuffle with the full list of ministers.

sections.title: The Diet
sections.summary: The House of Representatives asserts the right to nominate a prime minister, the 92nd session is delayed, and 22 features of the unpassed Diet Law are listed.

sections.title: Summary of Ninety-first Extraordinary Diet Session
sections.summary: Statistics for the 31-day session of 26 November-26 December: 69 bills, 130 petitions, 12,269 visitors, Liberals at 148 seats, and a dissolution resolution defeated 256-160.

sections.title: The Constitution
sections.summary: Government plans to publicize the new Constitution before 3 May, with Daiei, Tano and Shochiku films and party women's committees led by Hanako Muraoka.

sections.title: The Purge
sections.summary: Ordinances of 4 January extend the purge to local government and key posts, with a screening schedule covering 80,700 persons and MacArthur's 31 January rebuttal of Newsweek.

sections.title: Local Government
sections.summary: A 21 January cabinet decision dissolves federations of tonari-gumi neighborhood associations by 1 April, with Home Minister Omura's statement, plus two personnel changes.

sections.title: Section 2. Public Safety
sections.summary: Orderly demonstrations including 150,000 workers at the Palace on 28 January, black-market raids, 143,090 offenses in November, the Police College opening, prison reform and winter fires.

sections.title: Law and Order
sections.summary: Demonstrations, attacks on labor leader Kikunami, black-market raids arresting 1,437 persons, smuggling from Formosa, and November crime statistics with prefectural rate charts.

sections.title: Public Casualties
sections.summary: Railway accidents including an electric train overturning near Imaichi on 7 January, Tokyo traffic restrictions, and seven deaths from methyl alcohol whiskey.

sections.title: Police
sections.summary: New police chiefs, the Police College opening at Ogikubo on 14 January with 200 students, radio patrol cars, and 24,537 juvenile offenses in Tokyo in 1946.

sections.title: Prisons
sections.summary: Ministry of Justice reform campaign of 15 January, a Muroran escape attempt, and prison population falling from 70,753 in November to 67,995 in December.

sections.title: Fire
sections.summary: 1,793 fires in December with 110 deaths, the Toyama fire destroying 350 houses on 2 January, Army fire losses and new theater fire rules.

sections.title: Section 3. Legal and War Crimes
sections.summary: Occupation court cases, 1,204 atrocity investigations on hand, 860 suspects interned at Sugamo, Yokohama and Philippine trials, and the Tokyo Tribunal prosecution resting on 24 January.

sections.title: Legal and Military Occupation Courts
sections.summary: Disposition of seven criminal cases involving UN nationals, five Japanese sentenced for typewriter theft in Yokohama, and acquittal of three police over the 19 July riot.

sections.title: Investigation of Suspected War Criminals
sections.summary: 118 new atrocity cases opened, 1,204 on hand, a Palawan Massacre survivor located, and Australian, British, Chinese and Philippine investigation results.

sections.title: Apprehension of Suspected War Criminals
sections.summary: Ten memorandums ordered 177 persons apprehended; 41 interned at Sugamo, bringing the total to 860; 22 suspects transferred to Australian and British custody.

sections.title: Prosecution of War Criminals
sections.summary: 116 defendants tried at Yokohama (11 death sentences), six trials completed in January, a Philippine total of 153 tried, and 44 executions at Rabaul.

sections.title: International Prosecution of War Criminals
sections.summary: Prosecution rested 24 January after nine months; extensive POW testimony on the Burma railway, Sandakan and Sumatra; defense motions for mistrial rejected 27 January.

sections.title: Part III: Economic
sections.summary: Agriculture through property control: farm and fisheries output, coal and power shortages, manufacturing and textiles, labor and the strike crisis, trade, rationing, finance and reparations.

sections.title: Section 1. Agriculture and Fisheries
sections.summary: 10,332 land commissions formed in December voting, 1946 staple food output of 18,477,000 tons, December landings of 121,214 tons and 422 whales caught in the Antarctic.

sections.title: Agriculture
sections.summary: Land commission elections, land reform pamphlets, wildlife conservation proposals, DDT toxicity to silkworms and radiation mutations in Nagasaki plants.

sections.title: Fisheries
sections.summary: December landings, 1946 marine products of 1,737,700 tons, Antarctic whaling by Taiyo and Nippon Suisan, petroleum allocations and 203 steel fishing ships built in 1946.

sections.title: Section 2. Forestry and Mining
sections.summary: December log output of 421,800,000 board feet, coal production of 2,172,900 tons, stockpiles of 925,000 tons on 20 January, and oil output of 16,958 kiloliters hampered by Akita snow.

sections.title: Forestry
sections.summary: Log output, 944 new sawmills, 20,000,000 board feet of relief lumber approved for earthquake victims, and charts for plywood, timber products and charcoal.

sections.title: Mining
sections.summary: Coal production, consumption and stockpiles, lignite, petroleum drilling and November mineral output, including copper content of 1,784 tons and iron ore at 50,826 tons.

sections.title: Section 3. Heavy Industries
sections.summary: Coke output of 108,000 tons, low metal production, 1,100 tons of crude rubber from Singapore on 20 January, shipbuilding approvals, chemicals at 35 percent of minimum, machine tools up six percent.

sections.title: Section 4. Manufacturing
sections.summary: Food processing short of soybeans, pulp up 100 percent for rayon, 1,261 trucks produced, rubber use falling to 907 tons, plus glass, leather and farm implements.

sections.title: Section 5. Textile Industries
sections.summary: Cotton yarn rose to 26,980,000 pounds, raw silk fell to 9,257 bales, rayon staple dropped by a third, and power restrictions limited wool, bast fibers and knit goods.

sections.title: Section 6. Transportation and Public Utilities
sections.summary: Rail fares raised 25 percent and freight 100 percent, 193,012 train-kilometers cancelled, freight down 689,700 tons, and power generation of 2,475,000,000 kilowatt hours under severe restrictions.

sections.title: Section 7. Communications
sections.summary: Telephone and telegraph trends, 495 radio stations, Tokyo-San Francisco radio programs authorized 17 January, expanded international mail, postal construction and Broadcasting Corporation finances.

sections.title: Section 8. Labor
sections.summary: 16,171 unions with 4,296,589 members, the 1 February strike threat, MacArthur's 31 January prohibition, the wage commission, wage limit raised to 700 yen, and unemployment and training.

sections.title: Labor Legislation
sections.summary: Draft bills on workmen's compensation, unemployment insurance, seamen and employment exchanges, and an 18 January ordinance barring wartime labor front leaders.

sections.title: Labor and Employer Organizations
sections.summary: Union statistics, Economic Reconstruction Conference preparations, formation of the 108,000-member Private Railway Workers federation, and teachers' union unification.

sections.title: Labor Relations
sections.summary: Government workers' strike plans, the Kikunami stabbing, failed negotiations, and the full text of MacArthur's 31 January statement prohibiting the general strike.

sections.title: Labor Education
sections.summary: Kanto Employers' Association labor school began 15 January with 300 students; union schools were postponed to April.

sections.title: Wages and Working Conditions
sections.summary: Wage rises in October-November, family expenditure of 1,017 yen biweekly, Wage Investigation Commission members, and temporary government worker raises of 150 yen plus 25 percent.

sections.title: Employment and Unemployment
sections.summary: Vocational training reached 331 centers, textile employment 493,762, coal miners up to 360,000, plus prevailing wage rules for public works and occupation labor.

sections.title: Section 9. Imports and Exports
sections.summary: First U.S. sugar and 54,811 bales of raw cotton imported; cotton yarn to Hongkong and Burma, fabrics to Korea, fish oil to the United States, locomotives and printing supplies to China and Korea.

sections.title: Section 10. Rationing and Price Control
sections.summary: 91.4 days of staple stocks, 73 percent of rice quota collected by 20 January, 55,000 tons of imported wheat released, a fertilizer bag shortage, and 88,973 violations.

sections.title: Food
sections.summary: Staple stock levels, rice collection incentives, supplementary rations for heavy laborers and fishermen, imported food releases, and fresh fish, vegetable and fruit supplies.

sections.title: Rents and Fertilizer
sections.summary: Rent increases in four of 24 major cities, 98 percent of land rents registered, and a 5,055,000-bag shortfall of straw bags for fertilizer.

sections.title: Fuel and Miscellaneous Goods
sections.summary: Coal deliveries at 98.6 percent of allocation, petroleum restriction enforcement, shoe prices up 10 to 30 percent and price indexes for leather and aluminum ware.

sections.title: Controls and Violations
sections.summary: Occupation supervision of fuel distribution, the 22 January ban on critical materials in nonessential goods, and hoarded goods worth 2,578,598 yen recovered in December.

sections.title: Section 11. Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Japan notes reached 100,040,145,000 yen, National City Bank remittance authority, 6,600,000,000 yen Treasury bills, national debt of 255,307,000,000 yen and Imperial Household downsizing.

sections.title: Money and Banking
sections.summary: National City Bank of New York authorized to handle US-to-Japan remittances; Bank of Japan notes hit 100,040,145,000 yen on 31 January. Bank of Japan notes issued rose from 78,049 to 92,433 million yen, 10 December to 10 January.

sections.title: Liquidation
sections.summary: Securities Co-ordinating Liquidation Committee created, two companies designated closed institutions, and liquidation proceeds of 1,968,564,000 yen to 30 November.

sections.title: Public Finance
sections.summary: Treasury bills and special account borrowings of 15,344,000,000 yen authorized, a national debt table, local pension withholding, and transfer of the Imperial Court Police.

sections.title: Section 12. Property Control and Reparations
sections.summary: German property of 61,819,318 yen, 2,528 looted-property reports, 257,322,281 dollars of precious metals, a 600,000,000 yen cotton loan, and the Philippine reparations mission's arrival.

sections.title: Property Control
sections.summary: Patent agreements, German and looted property, assets of 848 suspected war criminals, Butoku Kai assets, precious metals and the SCAP custody account.

sections.title: Antitrust and Cartels
sections.summary: Loans approved for fishing vessels and a fertilizer plant, a 600,000,000 yen cotton rehabilitation loan, holding company proxies, and coal worker housing ordinances.

sections.title: Reparations
sections.summary: Changes in designated plant listings, arrival of the five-man Philippine Reparations Mission, and a new head of the Central Liaison Office Reparations Division.

sections.title: Part IV: Social
sections.summary: Public health, welfare and education: earthquake relief, repatriation, communicable disease rates, nutrition surveys, vital statistics, school reforms and press comment on the cabinet and strike crises.

sections.title: Section 1. Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: 2,837,207 persons on public assistance, 1,321 dead in the earthquake, 1,472,613 Japanese awaiting repatriation, penicillin standards, diphtheria and typhus rates, nutrition and vital statistics.

sections.title: Welfare
sections.summary: Welfare payments of 144,053,679 yen, a second LARA shipment of 386 tons, the earthquake toll, Red Cross reorganization and repatriation figures.

sections.title: Hospital Administration
sections.summary: 3,047 hospitals with 216,354 beds on 20 December and SCAP's medical reference library for Japanese educators.

sections.title: Veterinary Affairs
sections.summary: Veterinary Education Council adopted minimum standards on 15 January, with a four-year course from 1948, plus meat and milk inspection and animal diseases.

sections.title: Supply
sections.summary: Penicillin testing rules, medical and dental supply output of 185,097,835 yen, typhus vaccine production, 78,350 needing prosthetics, DDT production and narcotics releases.

sections.title: Preventive Medicine
sections.summary: December disease rates and 1946 totals, including 87,737 dysentery and 31,141 typhus cases, venereal disease clinics, airfield quarantine and cyanide fumigation.

sections.title: Nutrition
sections.summary: November nutrition survey showing higher caloric intake after the rice ration increase, low protein, weight deviations and deficiency symptoms.

sections.title: Vital Statistics
sections.summary: December births 30.2 per 1,000, deaths 102,103, infant deaths up 47 percent, 9,350 stillbirths, 64,393 marriages and 6,627 divorces.

sections.title: Section 2. Education, Religion and Media of Expression
sections.summary: Educational Reform Committee's second report, Constitution lecture courses, school lunches for 2,942 schools, missionary policy, a Nara cultural sites map and press comment on the strike.

sections.title: Education
sections.summary: Educational Reform Committee's 27 December report, Constitution lectures at 55 schools, Citizens' Public Halls subsidies, the school lunch program and an educational film committee.

sections.title: Religion
sections.summary: Liberalized missionary clearance policy and arrival of Greek Orthodox, Church of Christ and Nazarene survey representatives.

sections.title: Arts and Monuments
sections.summary: American art restoration publications passed to the Ministry of Education and no serious earthquake damage to arts; a Nara Prefecture cultural sites map follows.

sections.title: Media of Expression
sections.summary: Information programs on women, prisons, typhus and the Constitution, radio programs, Tokyo and prefectural press comment on the coalition and strike, magazines, theater and library attendance.

sections.title: Map of Japan
sections.summary: Final page with a map of Japan, followed by the National Archives and Records Service stamp.
